content: Anthrax is a severe illness caused by the bacterium Bacillus anthracis, which naturally exists in soil worldwide. It primarily affects livestock and wild animals, but humans can contract the disease through contact with infected animals or contaminated animal products. People may become infected by inhaling anthrax spores, consuming food or water contaminated with spores, or through spores entering cuts or abrasions on the skin. Livestock and wild animals, such as cattle, sheep, goats, antelope, and deer, can also become infected by ingesting or inhaling spores from contaminated soil, plants, or water. Although anthrax is rare in the United States, sporadic outbreaks occur in grazing animals like cattle or deer. In areas with a history of anthrax, veterinarians recommend annual vaccination of livestock. While most individuals are unlikely to encounter anthrax, certain occupations, hobbies, or activities may increase the risk of exposure. The type of anthrax infection depends on how the bacteria enter the body. All forms of anthrax can be fatal if untreated, but they are treatable with antibiotics. There are four main types of anthrax: 1. Cutaneous Anthrax: This occurs when anthrax spores enter the skin through cuts or abrasions, often during the handling of infected animals or contaminated products like wool, hides, or hair. It typically appears on the head, neck, forearms, or hands. Symptoms include itchy blisters or bumps, significant swelling around the sore, and a painless sore with a black center. This is the most common and least dangerous form of anthrax. A related condition, injection anthrax, has been observed in heroin users in Europe, causing deep infections at injection sites, but it has not been reported in the United States. 2. Inhalation Anthrax: This is the most lethal form of anthrax and occurs when spores are inhaled. It often affects individuals working in environments like wool mills, slaughterhouses, or tanneries where they may be exposed to infected animals or contaminated products. The infection begins in the lymph nodes of the chest and spreads throughout the body. Symptoms include fever, chills, heavy sweating, chest pain, cough, shortness of breath, confusion, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, headache, body aches, and extreme fatigue. 3. Gastrointestinal Anthrax: This rare form occurs when a person consumes raw or undercooked meat from an infected animal. It affects the upper gastrointestinal tract, stomach, and intestines. Symptoms include fever, chills, swollen neck or glands, sore throat, hoarseness, difficulty swallowing, nausea, vomiting (sometimes bloody), diarrhea (sometimes bloody), headache, red eyes, stomach pain, swelling, and fainting. 4. Welder’s Anthrax: This newly identified and rare form of anthrax has been observed in welders and metalworkers. It causes severe pneumonia and can be fatal. Symptoms include fever, chills, sudden cough, chest pain, difficulty breathing, and coughing up blood. Welders or metalworkers experiencing these symptoms should seek immediate medical attention. If you suspect exposure to anthrax, it is critical to contact a healthcare provider immediately and explain the circumstances of your potential exposure. Prompt medical care is essential for recovery. Antibiotics can prevent illness if administered early or treat the infection if symptoms have already developed. There is no diagnostic test to confirm exposure to anthrax; public health authorities must investigate to determine the source and extent of exposure.
